title: How Likely Is That?
blurb: Say how likely something is to happen

steps.html:
Virtual holidays. Printed meals. People finally getting tired of screens. Two speakers rate three predictions, and disagree about all of them — politely, and with about nine different ways of saying 'probably'.

  • Hear how sure a speaker is about a prediction
  • Use likely to, bound to, sure to, might and doubt
  • Watch an interview about how work is changing
  • Write a balanced opinion essay

steps.title: Language noticing.
steps.sub: 'I wouldn't be surprised if it happened.'
steps.prompt: Why is the past form used after if here?
options: Because the speaker is talking about the past.
Because this is a hypothetical future — the past form makes it less certain.
Because if is always followed by a past tense.
steps.answer: Because this is a hypothetical future — the past form makes it less certain.
steps.why: Moving the verb back one step in time is how English marks distance from reality, not distance in time.

steps.title: From bound to happen to no chance at all
steps.html:
A recycled area: the future forms from Lessons 17 and 18, plus the language that grades them.

English rarely says probably twice in a paragraph. It grades likelihood with a range of structures, and each one has a fixed shape you have to get right.

be bound to / be sure to + infinitive = you are confident it will happen. It's bound to happen. That's sure to happen.

be likely to + infinitive = probable. The negative is unlikely to, not not likely in careful writing. We are likely to have more automation.

might / may / could + infinitive = possible, no more. I suppose it might happen.

I expect / I doubt + clause. Note that doubt is followed by a positive clause: I doubt people would be satisfied, not I doubt people wouldn't be satisfied.

I wouldn't be surprised if + past form, and there's no chance of + -ing. Both are fixed: I wouldn't be surprised if it happened. There's no chance of me eating that.

steps.title: Example bank.
steps.html:
Ten sentences, most of them straight from the recording.

I think it's bound to happen.
Confident. Infinitive after bound to.

Oh, that's sure to happen.
Equally confident.

We are likely to have more and more automation.
Probable.

Trains are unlikely to have drivers by then.
The negative of likely.

I expect they'll just travel more within their own countries.
Expect + a full clause.

I suppose it might happen.
Doubly hedged — the weakest thing in the recording.

I still doubt people would be satisfied.
Positive clause after doubt.

I wouldn't be surprised if it happened.
Past form after if for a hypothetical future.

There's no chance of me eating something like that.
-ing after of.

You may be right about that, but …
Concede, then disagree. The most useful move in the lesson.

steps.title: Grading the same prediction four ways
steps.html:
1. The prediction: most holidays will be taken in virtual reality.
  2. If you are confident: It's bound to happen. Infinitive after bound to.
  3. If you think it probable: Virtual holidays are likely to become normal. Again an infinitive.
  4. If you think it merely possible: It might happen. No to after might.
  5. If you think it will not: I doubt people would be satisfied with it. Note the clause after doubt is positive — the doubting is already done by the verb.

steps.title: The Future of Work
steps.sub: The Future of Work. About seven minutes.

steps.title: Answer the questions about the interview.
steps.prompt: What does he name as the biggest change of the past decade?
steps.why: 'I think the big change has been technology.' It has shut some industries down and made others more accessible.

steps.title: Answer the questions about the interview.
steps.prompt: What example does he give of a skill that used to be rare?
options: Writing HTML code or building a website
steps.answer: Writing HTML code or building a website
steps.why: Ten years ago it was a rare skill; now it is part of a marketing or admin role.

steps.title: Answer the questions about the interview.
steps.prompt: What does 'agile working' mean in his description?
options: Working faster than before, with shorter deadlines throughout.
Not being tied to one desk — perhaps three or four days in the office and the rest elsewhere.
Working entirely from home, with no office to go back to.
steps.answer: Not being tied to one desk — perhaps three or four days in the office and the rest elsewhere.
steps.why: He mentions working from an iPad in a coffee shop as an example.

steps.title: Answer the questions about the interview.
steps.prompt: Who does he say may find the new practices unsettling?
options: The younger generation, who are internet natives
More mature workers, used to their own workspace
steps.answer: More mature workers, used to their own workspace
steps.why: 'Not having their own set workspace, not having their own files around them.'

steps.title: Read between the lines.
steps.prompt: Why does he say he would be a very rich man if he could predict the future?
options: He is refusing to answer the question.
He is hedging: he will give an opinion, but wants it understood as an opinion.
He thinks the question is unfair.
steps.answer: He is hedging: he will give an opinion, but wants it understood as an opinion.
steps.why: He goes on to answer at length. The joke is a hedge, exactly like the phrases in the listening.

steps.title: Write a balanced opinion essay.
steps.sub: 180–220 words. Title: In twenty years, most office work will be done from home. Give both sides, then your own view.
steps.placeholder: Open with the claim you are going to examine.
steps.html:
• Open by stating the proposition and conceding something.
  • Give two arguments in favour, in one paragraph.
  • Give the arguments against, in the next.
  • Close with your own view, clearly marked as yours.
  • Grade every prediction: bound to, likely to, might, I doubt.

Useful language

  • It is often argued that … , and there is something in this.
  • Employers are likely to … , since …
  • It is bound to suit some people and unlikely to suit others.
  • I doubt that … would …
  • There is no chance of … disappearing altogether.
  • On balance, I would expect …
steps.modelHtml:
It is often argued that office work will move almost entirely into the home within twenty years, and there is something in this. The technology already exists, and companies running out of expensive office space are likely to take any excuse to use less of it.

There are two strong arguments in favour. The first is cost: an employer who needs half the desks pays half the rent. The second is that the generation now entering work has never known anything else, and is bound to expect flexibility rather than ask for it.

Against that, managers cannot see what they cannot see. Several of the people interviewed about this raise the same worry, and I doubt that any software would fully answer it. There is also no chance of the social side of work disappearing without cost; a great deal of what people learn at work, they learn by overhearing it.

On balance, I would expect a split week rather than a move home. Three days in an office is unlikely to satisfy anybody completely, which is usually a sign that it is what will happen.
